method: Tamura and Gabor Wavelet transform texture features are extracted from images to build a feature vector database. application_domain: Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) using texture features
results_summary: The paper evaluates five distance metrics for a CBIR system using Tamura and Gabor Wavelet texture features on two image databases (400 and 600 images, 4 classes). results_summary: The paper describes the construction of three virtual databases: TRISUB (~757,000 structures of trisubstituted monocyclic hydrocarbons), BIAD (2,255 unsubstituted bicyclic hydrocarbons), and GEMINI (38,219 molecules in 323,533 conformations from combinatorial chemistries). research_focus: An enhanced vector-based encoding algorithm for representing the chemical environment of carbon atoms, used to retrieve matching environments from a database and predict carbon-13 NMR chemical shifts.
method: Chemical environments are encoded as vectors where each dimension represents the collective influence of atoms at a given bond distance from the carbon atom. Database retrieval uses Euclidean distance comparison between vectors to find the closest matching environment. Parameter optimization (number of atom classes, aromatic handling, vector dimensionality, weighting exponent) is performed on a training set, then evaluated on a separate test set.
application_domain: NMR spectroscopy and chemical shift prediction for organic structure elucidation
results_summary: The enhanced encoding algorithm was tested on a database of 16,959 training and 4,240 test structures (38,568 carbons in the test set). The optimal 15-dimensional combined vector representation achieved a median mean absolute deviation of 1.30 ppm in predicted chemical shifts. Approximately 75% of chemical shifts in the test set were predicted within 2.0 ppm. Euclidean distance was confirmed as a good predictor of prediction quality, with matches below 0.1 distance generally yielding accurate predictions while distances above 1.0 typically gave poor results. The authors also identified specific encoding deficiencies, such as inability to distinguish ortho vs. meta positions in aromatic systems and failure to encode cis/trans configurations.
limitations: The algorithm does not distinguish between ortho and meta positions relative to a carbon in aromatic systems; Cis/trans configurations of double bonds are not taken into consideration; Conjugation of double bonds is not explicitly treated in the encoding; Much detailed connection information is lost by collapsing atoms at each bond distance into a single scalar value (dimensionality reduction); Solvent effects and other experimental factors are not accounted for; Some experimental data in the database contain incorrectly assigned shifts; The methodology focuses only on chemical shifts and does not simulate spectral line width or intensity
research_gaps: Further enhancements to the aromatic encoding scheme to distinguish ortho, meta, and para positions; Incorporation of cis/trans configuration information into the encoding; Treatment of additional aromatic systems beyond six-membered carbon rings; Explicit treatment of double bond conjugation effects; Exploration of alternative multi-vector schemes (e.g., using largest or smallest Z values at each bond distance); Combining the direct retrieval approach with empirical modeling for improved accuracy and generality; Simulation of spectral parameters beyond chemical shifts (line width, intensity)

results_summary: The paper combined multi-temporal remote sensing data, historical cartography, and field surveys within a GIS environment to identify palaeo-hydrographic features around the Luna archaeological site. research_focus: Automatic updating of building boundaries in a GIS vector database from high-resolution satellite imagery using SVM classification and model-based matching against existing building shapes
method: Binary SVM classification of pan-sharpened IKONOS imagery augmented with nDSM and NDVI bands to detect building patches, followed by model-based delineation where shape parameters (area, perimeter, major/minor axis, elongation, compactness, solidity) are used to select the best-matching building from the existing GIS database and rotate it to fit the detected patch
application_domain: GIS database updating and building extraction from satellite imagery
results_summary: The approach was tested in the Batikent district of Ankara, Turkey, using IKONOS imagery and an existing 1:1000-scale building database. SVM classification achieved 92.45% overall accuracy and a kappa coefficient of 0.8490 for building patch detection. results_summary: The paper describes the Term Vector Database, which maps page identifiers to pre-computed term vectors for all pages in the AltaVista index, enabling retrieval orders of magnitude faster than downloading pages via HTTP. limitations: Current compression techniques work mostly by eliminating redundancy within individual vectors, making it unlikely to achieve another factor of two reduction by continuing that path; The database lacks content information beyond term vectors, requiring complementary services like the Connectivity Server

research_focus: The influence of database accuracy (building layout geometry, electrical characteristics, base station locations) on the quality of two-dimensional ray-tracing-based radio propagation predictions in urban microcellular environments.
method: Ray-tracing prediction models (including reflection and diffraction) were run using building databases of varying accuracy (cadastre map, city map, 1:25000 scaled map) and with injected random errors in building geometry. Predictions were compared against field measurements to quantify sensitivity to database inaccuracies.
application_domain: Radio wave propagation modeling and urban microcell planning
results_summary: The paper quantified how inaccuracies in building geometry databases affect ray-tracing prediction accuracy in urban microcells. It found that predictions are more sensitive to errors in building corner (vertex) positions than to errors in building size, because corner errors change wall orientation. The most precise map (cadastre) yielded the best predictions, and the model was sensitive to the choice of reflection coefficient but not to small base station location variations. Error thresholds were established: 95% of building walls within 2 m or 95% of vertices within 1 m keeps the standard deviation increase below 1 dB. The study also confirmed that specular reflection per Fresnel law is an important propagation phenomenon in microcells.
limitations: The model does not consider trees or other neglected effects that may affect propagation; The study was conducted in a single specific environment (Bern), limiting generalizability; A scalar reflection coefficient independent of incidence angle decreases computation time but leads to less satisfactory predictions
research_gaps: Similar investigations in different environments are needed to determine how error thresholds depend on the environment; Effects of trees and other neglected phenomena need to be incorporated into the model

research_focus: Improving query execution performance in the VectorWise analytical database by introducing compressed execution techniques, specifically RLE-compressed execution with constant vectors and dictionary-encoded data processing.

results_summary: The paper demonstrates that 8 out of 10 On-Time benchmark queries benefit from constant vectors, with queries 0 and 9 achieving over 40% execution time reduction. method: The framework extracts color autocorrelogram, improved edge histogram descriptor (EHD), and compact micro-textures using the FRGMRF model with Bayesian approach; classifies the combined feature vectors with multi-class SVM; indexes them using a kD-tree; and performs final similarity matching with Minkowski distance of order 3, augmented by a relevance feedback mechanism.
application_domain: Color image retrieval (content-based image retrieval)
results_summary: The paper proposes a CBIR system that extracts color, shape, and texture features via an FRGMRF model with Bayesian approach, classifies them with multi-class SVM, and retrieves using Minkowski distance with relevance feedback. research_focus: Validating a novel method of encoding semantic vectors into feature tokens for inverted-index-based fulltext search engines, and evaluating its performance across diverse datasets (text embeddings and image descriptors) with different similarity measures.
method: Semantic vectors are encoded into 'feature tokens' that are indexed and searched using standard inverted-index-based IR systems (Elasticsearch, Lucene, Sphinx, Solr). The paper evaluates the impact of the number of best features selected and the page size on Precision@10, NDCG@10, and Avg. diff.@10 across multiple datasets with varying dimensionalities and representations.
application_domain: Text document retrieval (NLP/information retrieval) and image search (SIFT descriptors)
results_summary: The paper validates the vector encoding method on datasets including LSA, doc2vec, GloVe text representations and SIFT image descriptors. It shows that keeping only the 90 best features is nearly indistinguishable from using all features in terms of Precision@10, and that dimensionality below 200 significantly degrades retrieval quality. The method achieves an excellent approximation of the gold standard across all tested datasets, confirming its stability and generalizability. Increasing the page size consistently improves relevance at the cost of search performance. The doc2vec dataset showed unusually low Precision@10 due to high mutual similarity among document vectors lacking distinct feature peaks.
limitations: Low-dimensional vectors (≤100 dimensions) cause a significant drop in Precision@10; The doc2vec representation produces vectors with high mutual similarity and lack of distinguishing feature peaks, degrading retrieval precision; Reducing the number of features used for querying decreases the relevance of retrieved documents by all metrics
research_gaps: Tuning doc2vec parameters to better differentiate between documents could solve the low-precision issue observed on that dataset; Further increase in page size would lead to further improvements in relevance at the cost of performance, suggesting a trade-off space not fully explored

research_focus: Developing a 3D geometrical approach to match raster datasets (Digital Surface Models) with vector datasets (3D polygons) of buildings for geospatial data conflation, integration, and change detection.
method: Computing 3D similarity measures (Euclidean distance, 2D and 3D buffers) between pixels of a raster DSM and 3D polygons from a city model, producing four matching results per pixel (2D/3D with/without positional uncertainty), and analyzing the effect of buffer width parameters on matching accuracy.
application_domain: Geospatial data integration and 3D cadastre (matching building footprints from DSMs to 3D city model polygons)
results_summary: The paper proposes and applies a 3D geometrical matching method between raster building data (DSM) and vector 3D polygons from a city model. Results show that 3D matching achieves over 60% pixel inclusion and 84-89% polygon matching, while 2D matching achieves over 70% pixel inclusion and 77-92% polygon matching. The analysis of buffer width parameters reveals that 3D matching is more robust to adjacent polygon ambiguity than 2D matching, as height information disambiguates pixels near polygon borders. The approach also detects geometric discrepancies in the 3D city model (e.g., incorrect roof shapes), demonstrating its utility for data quality assessment and cadastre updating.
limitations: The method is limited to one-to-one correspondences between pixels and polygons; Poor geometrical definition of some roofs in the 3D city model (e.g., octagonal pyramid represented as prism, gable roof represented as flat roof) reduces 3D matching accuracy; The 2D buffer width parameter is very sensitive and must be selected carefully to avoid multiple assignations; Large height buffer values can cause problems when the height difference between adjacent polygons is small

relevance_reason: The paper is entirely about designing, implementing, and evaluating a new vector database system (Manu), making vector databases the main and sole subject of the work.
research_focus: Design and implementation of Manu, a cloud-native vector database management system for billion-scale vector collections, with a focus on long-term evolvability, tunable consistency, fine-grained elasticity, and high performance by relaxing traditional DBMS constraints on transaction complexity and data consistency.
method: Manu follows a 'log as data' paradigm, structuring the system as log publish/subscribe microservices with WAL and binlog as backbone services. Write components act as log publishers while read-only search and analytic components are independent subscribers. Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) and a delta consistency model simplify inter-component communication. Hardware-aware optimizations for CPUs, GPUs, and SSDs are applied, along with support for complex search semantics.
indexing_methods: vector quantization; inverted index; proximity graphs
application_domain: Recommendation, multimedia, language, medicine, security, drug discovery, e-commerce, video recommendation
results_summary: The paper presents Manu's architecture as a cloud-native vector database built around log-based publish/subscribe microservices, MVCC, and a delta consistency model to achieve fine-grained component decoupling. The system supports multiple indexing methods (vector quantization, inverted index, proximity graphs) with hardware-aware implementations for CPUs, GPUs, and SSDs. Manu was evaluated in three typical application scenarios to demonstrate its efficiency, elasticity, and scalability at billion-scale. The design relaxes complex transaction requirements in exchange for tunable consistency and per-component scalability, addressing feedback from over 1200 industry users collected over three years.
limitations: Manu is still far from perfect according to the authors; Current vector search index assumes a single type of storage (GPU memory, main memory, or disk); Existing vector search algorithms only explore some combinations of techniques for different components
research_gaps: Multi-way search: exploring how multiple search engines (vector, primary key, text) can interact and coordinate efficiently; Modularized algorithms: providing a unified framework for vector search allowing flexible combination of compression, indexing, and bucketing techniques; Hierarchical storage aware index: exploring indexes that jointly utilize all devices on the storage hierarchy; Advanced hardware: exploiting NVM, RDMA, NVLink, FPGA, and MLU for vector search and index building; Embedding generation toolbox: incorporating application-oriented toolbox with model fine-tuning and pre-trained models for rapid prototyping

research_focus: Designing a hybrid multi-layer intrusion detection system (IDS) for Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) healthcare networks that combines behaviour-based and anomaly-based detection with federated learning and interpretability.
method: A multi-layer architecture combining a Bloom filter-based behaviour detection module (layer 1) with an optimized SRU (Simple Recurrent Unit) anomaly detection layer (layer 2), trained via federated learning with dynamic parameter aggregation, and using LIME for interpretability of detection decisions.
application_domain: Cybersecurity and intrusion detection in IoMT-based smart healthcare networks
results_summary: The paper proposes a multi-layer IDS combining a Bloom filter-based behaviour module and an SRU-based anomaly detection layer for IoMT healthcare networks. The model achieved 99.27% accuracy, 99.28% precision, 98.73% recall, and 99.26% F1-score, outperforming LSTM, GRU, and other state-of-the-art approaches. The SRU model demonstrated superior handling of vanishing gradients with increasing network depth and faster training time compared to other RNN variants. LIME interpretability visualizations showed that feature F16 (related to IoMT/IoT device category) had the dominant impact on detection decisions. The federated learning approach with dynamic aggregation enabled real-time model updates across heterogeneous medical networks.

results_summary: The paper identifies five fundamental obstacles to vector data management (ambiguous similarity, expensive comparisons, large vector size, lack of structural properties, and hybrid query incompatibility) and surveys the techniques developed to overcome them. The survey characterizes existing VDBMSs along a spectrum from native mostly-vector systems (high performance, limited capability) to extended relational systems (most capability, potentially lower performance), noting that native mostly-mixed systems like Milvus, Qdrant, and Manu achieve a comfortable balance. It highlights that hybrid query processing, cost estimation for predicated queries, and effective vector partitioning for distributed systems remain open challenges. The paper concludes by pointing toward future systems that combine high performance with unified data management capabilities and more efficient disk-resident indexes.

research_focus: Comparison of insertion and query performance of three open-source vector databases (Chroma, Qdrant, Faiss) on datasets of varying sizes (10,000 to 9,990,000 vectors) from the Deep1B dataset.
method: Vectors from the Deep1B dataset were sequentially inserted into Chroma, Qdrant, and Faiss at ten different sizes. Insertion times (including indexing) and query times (top-10 nearest neighbor search on 1000 randomly selected vectors) were measured on an M1 Max processor with 64 GB RAM. Default similarity metrics were used per database (Squared L2 for Chroma, Cosine for Qdrant, L2 for Faiss). No metadata, replication, or partitioning was applied.
application_domain: General vector similarity search for high-dimensional deep learning embeddings
results_summary: The paper measured insertion and query performance of Chroma, Qdrant, and Faiss across dataset sizes from 10,000 to 9,990,000 vectors. Faiss exhibited the fastest insertion times due to its in-memory operation, while Chroma and Qdrant showed increasing insertion times with growing data volume due to index growth. For queries, Faiss provided optimal performance on small datasets without requiring an index, but its advantage diminished as data size increased due to growing memory requirements. Chroma's disk-based storage and indexing capabilities made it more suitable for larger datasets where memory constraints are a concern. Qdrant in memory showed similar insertion times to its disk-based counterpart, indicating that the in-memory configuration did not significantly improve insertion speed.
limitations: No replication or partitioning was performed on the databases; Vectors were added without metadata, limiting the evaluation to pure vector performance; Only one hardware configuration (M1 Max, 64 GB RAM) was used for all measurements; No swap operation with disk was performed, restricting results to in-memory scenarios for Faiss and Qdrant
research_gaps: Deeper investigation of nuanced performance characteristics across various configurations; Exploration of sharding, partitioning, and replication strategies for optimizing database performance

application_domain: Image data security (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CelebA, CIFAR10) in the context of vector database privacy

relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a novel compression method for Product Quantization codebooks, which is a core indexing technology underlying vector databases and ANN search. It directly proposes, analyzes, and benchmarks improvements to a fundamental component of vector database systems.
research_focus: Lossless compression of Product Quantization (PQ) codebooks to reduce memory footprint of vector databases, enabling deployment of ANN-based retrieval on resource-constrained edge devices.
method: SegPQ compresses PQ codebooks by (1) projecting codewords to integer sorting keys via binary concatenation (BinCat), (2) reordering the codebook to fit an optimal Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) model under an error constraint ε, and (3) storing the residuals between PLA predictions and true codewords together with the line segments as the compressed codebook. Theoretical analysis establishes coverage bounds for the ε-PLA model without relying on the gap model used by PGM-Index.
indexing_methods: Product Quantization (PQ); Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH); Proximity Graph; Vector Quantization; k-means clustering
application_domain: LLM-enhanced applications (RAG, open-domain question answering) on resource-constrained edge devices; web-scale vector search
results_summary: SegPQ robustly achieves the highest compression ratio among all baselines and is the only method that keeps memory below 1 GiB for 1 billion vectors. Construction overhead is negligible (less than 3.4% of PQ training time), and query overhead is under 6% of overall ANN query processing. Compared to the state-of-the-art DeltaPQ, SegPQ demonstrates superiority in memory footprint, construction efficiency, and query efficiency simultaneously. Theoretical results confirm that SegPQ maintains comparable asymptotic performance even under non-uniform codebook distributions.
limitations: BinCat projection generates excessively large value spaces for high-bit-width codebooks (e.g., PQ128/PQ256), impairing learned PLA efficacy; Codeword reordering inevitably modifies original vector ID assignments, requiring a generic scenario assumption that IDs can be safely updated; For high-bit-width codebooks, only partial compression (upper 64 bits) is supported, yielding lower compression ratios (1.43× for PQ128, 1.18× for PQ256)
research_gaps: Embedding SegPQ into prevalent VectorDB engines to facilitate seamless integration of vector search on edge devices; Further theoretical analysis of SegPQ under non-uniform codebook distributions (generalized bound provided but full treatment deferred to technical report)

research_focus: Building a scalable, high-performance, and cost-efficient vector search system inside a cloud-native operational database (Azure Cosmos DB) by deeply integrating the DiskANN vector indexing library, as an alternative to specialized vector databases that require data replication.

application_domain: General-purpose operational database workloads including e-commerce, document retrieval, conversational histories, AI agent interaction, web search, and recommendation systems
results_summary: The paper demonstrates that integrating DiskANN into Azure Cosmos DB achieves approximately 20ms query latency at 10 million vector scale while offering 43× lower query cost than Pinecone and 12× lower than Zilliz serverless enterprise products. research_focus: Designing a dedicated index for range-filtering approximate nearest neighbor search (RFANNS) in vector databases that supports fully incremental construction and handles arbitrary range filters with varying query selectivity and correlation.
method: The paper proposes WoW, a window graph-based RFANNS index that builds hierarchical window graphs with varying window sizes using a Window-Based Tree (WBT) for incremental insertion. For querying, it employs query selectivity to select the most relevant window graphs and combines multiple window graphs to recover missing edges relative to the oracle proximity graph. Theoretical analysis provides time complexity bounds and optimal parameter settings.
indexing_methods: window graph; hierarchical window graphs; oracle proximity graph; RNG (Relative Neighbor Graph); hashing-based ANNS; partition-based ANNS; graph-based ANNS; WBT (Window-Based Tree)
application_domain: Vector database management systems; examples include e-commerce image search with price filtering and medical RAG question answering with age-range filtering
results_summary: The paper proposes WoW, a fully incremental window graph-based index for RFANNS, and evaluates it against existing baselines on real-world datasets. For index construction, WoW's indexing time is on par with the most building-efficient baseline and 4.9× faster than the most query-efficient index (DIGRA) while being 0.4-0.5× smaller in size. For RFANNS queries, WoW is 4× faster than the best incremental index and 1.5× faster than the best statically-built index on high-selectivity workloads, with equal or better performance on other workloads. The paper also proves that insertion time complexity is O(log²n) and query time complexity is O(log n'), matching the oracle RNG bound.
limitations: The index only supports single-attribute range filtering, not multi-attribute filtering; In-place update and deletion of existing entries are not yet supported
research_gaps: Extending WoW to multi-attribute range filtering; Adding in-place update and deletion support to WoW

application_domain: E-commerce product search, recommendation systems, face recognition, text retrieval, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for large language models
results_summary: The paper formalizes the Elastic Index Selection (EIS) problem for label-hybrid AKNN search, proves it is NP-complete, and proposes greedy algorithms for two optimization variants. research_focus: The paper addresses the resource inefficiency of existing distributed ANNS solutions that rely on segmentation-based (MapReduce-style) approaches, and proposes a new RDMA-enabled distributed framework (RED-ANNS) that maintains a logically full graph index across multiple nodes for more efficient large-scale vector search.
method: RED-ANNS uses an RDMA network to create a shared memory space across multiple nodes, maintains a full Vamana/DiskANN graph index spanning all nodes, and employs locality-aware data placement, affinity-based query scheduling, and a dependency-relaxed best-first search algorithm with data prefetching to reduce and hide remote access overhead.

relevance_reason: The paper proposes a learned cardinality estimation model specifically designed for vector database query optimization, addressing challenges unique to vector databases (hybrid queries, ANNS + predicate filtering, graph-based indexes), and is evaluated on a vector database system (DingoDB). However, the main subject is the ML-based estimation technique rather than vector databases as a whole, making it a substantial but not sole focus.
research_focus: Accurate cardinality estimation for complex predicate filtering queries in vector databases, specifically for hybrid queries combining scalar metadata filtering with approximate nearest neighbor search, to improve query plan selection in vector database optimizers.
method: A Tree-LSTM-based architecture that encodes the hierarchical structure of nested Boolean predicates (AST alignment) combined with a domain-aware metadata and predicate encoding scheme, augmented with an Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) based incremental learning mechanism to adapt to evolving data distributions without full retraining.
application_domain: Vector database query optimization for hybrid queries (predicate filtering + ANNS), with applications in semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation, and recommendation.
results_summary: VecCard was evaluated on two real-world datasets (MOOCCubeX and Yelp) integrated into the DingoDB vector database. It achieved a Mean Q-Error of 1.91 and Median Q-Error of 1.29 on Yelp, representing a 70% reduction in average error compared to the strongest structural baseline (TreeRNN). On the sparser MOOCCubeX dataset, VecCard maintained a stable Mean Q-Error of 5.77 while traditional estimators degraded to errors in the tens or hundreds. When integrated into DingoDB's native optimizer, VecCard significantly reduced query latency and resource consumption across heterogeneous index structures such as HNSW and IVF_FLAT. The EWC-based incremental learning mechanism enabled adaptation to distribution shifts without catastrophic forgetting.
research_gaps: Extending VecCard to support complex multi-table join scenarios in enterprise-level multimodal databases; Transitioning from pure cardinality estimation to end-to-end cost model learning that directly predicts nonlinear hardware execution costs for traversing vector graph indexes; Exploring federated learning paradigms for cardinality estimation in distributed vector databases to address privacy-sensitive AI applications

research_focus: Accelerating graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (specifically HNSW) by addressing the memory-bandwidth bottleneck through a software-hardware co-optimized architecture that combines scalar quantization with re-ranking while preserving full-precision accuracy.
method: A bit-partitioned vector search framework using 8-bit partitioned quantization applied to both graph traversal and re-ranking phases, combined with a unified hardware accelerator that shares computational resources across both phases and a redesigned memory data layout to minimize hardware and memory overhead.

application_domain: Recommendation systems, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search engines, and natural language processing
results_summary: The paper proposes BAGS, a software-hardware co-optimized architecture that applies 8-bit partitioned quantization in both the HNSW graph traversal and re-ranking phases to alleviate memory bandwidth saturation. research_focus: Efficient processing of hybrid vector search queries that combine approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) retrieval with predicate filtering on structured data attributes, specifically proposing a metadata-agnostic, popularity-aware approach using proximity graph structures.
method: The approach constructs clusters from the base layer of HNSW graphs and maintains in-memory sketches (count-min sketch for point queries, CDF-based regression model for range filtering) populated with attribute values from nodes. During search, the nearest neighbor of the query vector is identified, and a two-hop search is conditionally triggered based on the popularity of the specific predicate within the corresponding cluster.
indexing_methods: HNSW; Product Quantization (PQ); Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH); Inverted File Index (IVF); Proximity Graph (PG)-based approaches; Count-Min Sketch; CDF-based regression model
application_domain: General-purpose hybrid vector search combining semantic similarity retrieval with structured attribute filtering (illustrated with a medical X-ray scan example)
results_summary: The paper proposes a popularity-aware hybrid vector search solution that uses HNSW base-layer clusters with in-memory sketches to decide whether to perform a two-hop search based on predicate popularity. Experiments on five real-world datasets, focusing on low-selectivity queries where pre-filtering is inefficient, show that the proposed approach outperforms alternative PG-based and other ANN-based methods. The solution also demonstrates greater robustness compared to existing techniques. The method remains metadata-agnostic, avoiding the need for separate graph structures per attribute or modifications to the original graph.
